analysis.investment_thesis: Aarti Drugs is a commodity API manufacturer whose COVID-era supercycle has fully reversed — revenues have declined two consecutive years (₹2,716 Cr → ₹2,387 Cr) and net profit has nearly halved from the 2021 peak of ₹280 Cr to ₹168 Cr. At 6.16% operating margins and 12.7% ROE, this business fails the fundamental quality thresholds needed for a long-term India compounder.
key_strengths: Manageable leverage at 0.39 D/E with stable promoter holding at 55%
Diversified API portfolio across analgesics, antibiotics, antifungals, and antidiabetics reduces single-product risk
OCF positive in all 5 of last 5 years, active capex cycle (CWIP ₹179 Cr) may unlock future capacity
key_risks: Revenue declining for 2 consecutive years — from ₹2,716 Cr (FY23) to ₹2,387 Cr (FY25), signalling structural pricing pressure in commodity APIs
Margin compression severe: EBITDA fell from ₹490 Cr (FY21) to ₹307 Cr (FY25) on heavier capital base — capex of ₹152–226 Cr/yr not generating returns
ROE 12.7% and ROCE 13.1% both below my 15% minimum, with rising finance costs (₹26 Cr in FY21 → ₹39 Cr in FY25) despite no meaningful debt reduction
red_flags: Net profit has collapsed 40% from FY21 peak (₹280 Cr → ₹168 Cr) while the stock is priced for recovery that hasn't materialised
Free cash flow barely positive (₹67 Cr FY25) despite ₹245 Cr OCF — heavy capex consuming all operational cash generation
Cash on books only ₹5 Cr against total debt of ₹615 Cr — thin liquidity buffer in a margin-pressured environment
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Aarti Drugs is a textbook example of what happens when a commodity API business rides a supercycle and then gets exposed. The FY2021 peak — ₹440 Cr operating income, ₹280 Cr PAT — was driven by COVID-era demand and supply chain disruptions globally. Since then, the business has given back most of those gains: FY25 operating income of ₹290 Cr is actually below FY20 levels of ₹266 Cr, while the asset base has grown from ₹1,576 Cr to ₹2,612 Cr. That is precisely the wrong direction — more capital, less earnings. Revenue CAGR of 8.6% over 9 years is below my 12% minimum, and the last 2-year trend is outright negative. For me, a business must be growing to deserve capital allocation.

The quality metrics tell the same uncomfortable story. A 6.16% operating margin in pharma is low — quality API businesses should be running 12-18%. ROE of 12.7% and ROCE of 13.1% mean shareholders are not being rewarded for capital employed. The heavy capex cycle (₹226 Cr in FY24, ₹177 Cr in FY25) has created a large CWIP that is yet to translate into earnings accretion. At 16.8x P/E, the valuation looks superficially reasonable, but it is pricing in a recovery in margins and volumes that may be structurally difficult given Chinese API competition and domestic pricing pressure. I need a business that is expanding its moat, not defending shrinking margins. India's pharma opportunity is real, but I would rather own a formulations company with pricing power or a CDMO with long-term contracts — not a commodity API manufacturer struggling to earn its cost of capital.
